note: EXP-0004 code reading: three readers (scheduler, CUDA backend, MoE graph) and two adversarial verifiers each. Level 2 evidence.

reader.summary: From the code, the expert upload during generation is serialized with GPU compute. Nothing overlaps them. The MoE cache turns pipeline parallelism off, so the scheduler runs with n_copies=1 and has no events. Every split input copy therefore begins with a full ggml_backend_synchronize, which on CUDA is cudaStreamSynchronize on the single backend stream. One generated token runs 42 splits: 1 CPU split (token-embedding get_rows), 1 CUDA split (layer 0 attention up to its router and top-k), and 40 CUDA splits that each start at layer il's slot-map lookup and run through layer il+1's router and top-k. The 42 matches the existing log line "splits = 122 / 42, ... sched copies = 1". At each MoE boundary the steps are in this order. (1) The host has already queued split S(il-1) asynchronously: routed experts of layer il-1, shared expert, layer il attention, router and top-k. (2) The scheduler moves to S(il), copies its only host-weight input (the slot map), and calls ggml_backend_synchronize first, so the host blocks until the whole of S(il-1) has finished on the device. (3) The copy callback (llama_moe_cache::copy) queues a 32-byte device-to-host read of the selected ids and synchronizes again (second host block, device idle). (4) The host plans hits and fills in the SLRU. (5) It issues one cudaMemcpyAsync per run of missing experts for each of the 3 expert tensors (gate, up, down), then the slot-map upload, all on the same compute stream. (6) Only after the callback returns does the scheduler call graph_compute_async for S(il). The device then runs in stream order: uploads, slot map, lookup, routed MUL_MAT_ID, shared expert, residual, next layer's attention, router, top-k. So the host waits on the device twice per MoE layer (80 per token, plus a few input-copy syncs at token start and the final logits sync). The device waits on the host once per MoE layer (40 per token): it sits idle from the end of S(il-1) until the first upload is queued, and the compute units are idle while the uploads run. The scheduler issues split S(il)'s work only after the callback returns, and the callback starts only after S(il-1) has drained, so host and device work in lockstep with no run-ahead. The only work that could legally overlap layer il's upload without speculation is: (a) layer il's shared expert and its sigmoid gate, which depend only on attn_post_norm but are built after the routed MoE, so they sit in S(il) behind the uploads; and (b) the routed matmul over experts already resident in VRAM (hits), if MUL_MAT_ID were split into a hit part and a miss part. Nothing from layer il+1 can overlap, because its attention and router need layer il's output, so cross-layer overlap needs speculative prefetch. A rough estimate, not measured: the shared expert is 2048x512x3, about the size of one routed expert (about 1.8 MiB), roughly 7 us of compute, against roughly 140 us or more of PCIe 4.0 x8 time per missed expert. The legal window is therefore tiny next to the upload. For the overlap to happen at all, the uploads would need their own stream plus an event, and both whole-stream syncs (ggml-backend.cpp:1844 and llama-moe-cache.cpp:846) would need to become event waits on the top-k. CUDA graphs: the CPU split cannot use them. Each of the 41 CUDA splits is eligible: graphs are keyed per split by nodes[0], MUL_MAT_ID with one token goes through MMVQ and needs no sync, and the uploads are queued before capture starts. Graphs only cut launch overhead, though; they do not remove the per-layer sync gap.

missed: GGML_CUDA_REGISTER_HOST changes no code path in the scheduler, the copy callback, the stream choice or CUDA graph eligibility. The expert buffers keep their CPU buffer type, so ggml_backend_sched_is_host_weight and the cudaMemcpyAsync calls at ggml-cuda.cu:2652 are identical either way. Only the driver's behaviour for the expert uploads changes. Unset (the default, and what EXP-0001 ran with: collect.sh:33 sets only LLAMA_MOE_CACHE_TRACE): the source is pageable mmap memory and each cudaMemcpyAsync may be staged and block the host. Set: pin_host_experts (llama-moe-cache.cpp:641-740) calls cudaHostRegister with Portable|ReadOnly (ggml-cuda.cu:5426), capped by default at total_ram/4 (llama-moe-cache.cpp:712). Ranges past the cap stay pageable (725-727). With 18760 MiB of host experts (log_prompt.txt:2120), full pinning needs more than about 73 GiB of RAM or a raised LLAMA_MOE_PIN_MIB. Below that, the run mixes pinned and pageable layers.

When the experts are pinned, cudaMemcpyAsync returns at once. The host can then enqueue or launch S(il)'s kernels or CUDA graph while the DMA runs. That hides launch overhead under the upload, but there is still no device compute overlap. So the 'no run-ahead' statement holds only for pageable memory. One caveat: the trailing slot-map upload always comes from pageable memory (llama-moe-cache.cpp:550, 594). Per the CUDA docs, the driver 'may synchronize with the stream' to stage it, which could make the host wait for the pinned uploads anyway. The code cannot settle this; it is runtime behaviour.

Changing streams and events alone cannot create the overlap the reader proposes. The shared expert must also move ahead of the lookup cut in graph order, after top-k il, because S(il) is enqueued only after the callback returns. The ids readback (llama-moe-cache.cpp:845) must not be queued on stream 0 behind it. It needs an event recorded after top-k plus a read on another stream or into mapped memory.

Banks are shared by all layers of a group: 36 layers share the q5_K bank (log_prompt.txt:2121). plan() picks victims across those layers and rewrites other layers' host slot maps (llama-moe-cache.cpp:240-241). Any asynchronous upload stream must therefore order its writes after layer il-1's routed matmul, a write-after-read hazard on reused slots. An event after top-k il covers this, since that matmul comes earlier in stream order. The host-side slot-map edits are safe today only because of the full syncs and the pageable staging.

LLAMA_MOE_CACHE_TRACE fprintf calls (llama-moe-cache.cpp:877-879) run inside the callback, after the expert uploads are queued but before the slot-map upload and before S(il) is launched. That is on the critical path. EXP-0001 ran with tracing on (collect.sh:33), which matters when interpreting its timings.

On Windows a GeForce card runs under WDDM, which batches command submission. Launch and sync latencies, and so the per-layer idle gap, can be larger than the code alone suggests. This is a runtime factor the code cannot settle.

reader.summary: In the shipping configuration (no GGML_CUDA_REGISTER_HOST), the expert uploads are serialized with GPU compute. Two separate things are serialized: host and GPU timing, and stream order. ggml_backend_cuda_set_tensor_async, get_tensor_async and synchronize all use cuda_ctx->stream(), which is stream(device, curr_stream_no). That is one lazily created cudaStreamNonBlocking stream per backend. curr_stream_no is 0 everywhere except inside a graph_compute fork/join region, which is opt-in through GGML_CUDA_GRAPH_OPT=1 and is joined back to stream 0 before the split ends. So the D2H read of the router ids, every H2D expert upload, the H2D slot-map upload and the next split's kernels or CUDA-graph launch are all queued in order on stream 0. A stream never runs a copy and a kernel at the same time, so nothing overlaps on the GPU. The host also blocks twice per MoE layer before any upload starts. First, the scheduler synchronizes the stream before copying a split input: its events are NULL because pipeline parallelism (n_copies>1) is off when the MoE cache is on or there is only one device. Second, copy() calls get_tensor_async and then ggml_backend_synchronize. The GPU therefore sits idle during the readback and the hit/fill planning. Both the expert source (the mmap) and the slot map (a CPU buffer) are pageable. CUDA documents that a pageable async copy "might be synchronous with respect to host" and that the driver may stage it into pinned memory. In practice the host thread is held for most of each upload, and it only queues the next split once the uploads have been staged. With GGML_CUDA_REGISTER_HOST=1 the copy code is unchanged: same cudaMemcpyAsync, same stream. pin_host_experts calls cudaHostRegister(Portable|ReadOnly) on the page-aligned, merged expert ranges, capped by default at RAM/4; ranges that are refused or over the cap stay pageable. For the pinned ranges the copy becomes a direct DMA that does not block the host, so the host can queue the slot map and the next split's launches behind it. The GPU still runs copy then compute in stream order, so pinning only removes the host-side staging time and launch time and raises the transfer speed. It does not create copy/compute overlap. Without code changes, no copy-engine concurrency between an expert upload and a kernel is possible. No API, setting or environment variable sends set_tensor_async to another stream. Events are implemented but the scheduler never creates them in this configuration. The only other host-to-device stream is cudaStreamPerThread, which the buffer-level set_tensor uses and then synchronizes on the host; the cache does not use it. Work that could legally overlap layer il's upload, because it does not depend on the uploaded weights, is the shared expert of layer il, the routed experts that were cache hits, and a speculative prefetch for layer il+1. Using any of them needs code changes: a pinned source, a dedicated copy stream (up to 8 stream slots per device exist), an event recorded after the uploads and waited on before MUL_MAT_ID, and the independent work queued ahead of that wait. Today the shared expert is built after build_moe_ffn, so it lands in the split after the lookup, behind the uploads.

reader.summary: For this model (arch qwen35moe; n_embd 2048, 256 experts, top-8, n_ff_exp 512, n_ff_shexp 512, separate gate/up/down expert tensors), the code fully serializes the expert upload with GPU compute. Per layer, the router (ffn_gate_inp f32 [2048,256] matmul, softmax, argsort/top-k view, get_rows of the weights, then sum_rows/clamp/div, then ggml_cont of the ids) runs in the earlier split. The scheduler starts a new split at the get_rows slot-map lookup, because that lookup reads a host-weight tensor. Before running the copy callback it calls ggml_backend_synchronize: events are NULL because pipeline parallelism is turned off when the MoE cache is on. The callback reads the 8 ids back and synchronizes again, then queues the missing experts with cudaMemcpyAsync on the same CUDA stream that runs compute. Only after it returns is the split graph launched. While the upload runs no kernel is executing, and every kernel of the split waits behind it. That split holds the routed mul_mat_ids, the weighted sum, the shared expert, the residual add, all of layer il+1's attention or GDN, and router il+1. Between top-k and the bank-reading mul_mat_ids, only the weights post-processing (already done before the sync) and the shared expert FFN plus its sigmoid gate do not depend on the routed experts. The shared expert reads only attn_post_norm(il) and is joined by add(moe_out, ffn_shexp), but in node order it comes after the routed matmuls. In size it matches one routed expert: gate+up [2048x512] plus down [512x2048], 3.15M MAC. That is about 1/8 of the routed FLOPs (25.2M MAC) and about 22% of the routed weight bytes (about 3.19 MiB if q8_0, vs 14.5 MiB for 8 q4_K/q5_K experts at 1.8125 MiB each). Layer il+1 depends on the routed output of il: ffn_out = moe_out + shexp, l_out = ffn_out + residual, inpL = l_out, and attn_norm(il+1) reads inpL. Its shared expert depends on it as well, through attn_post_norm(il+1). Without prediction, the device work that could legally run during layer il's upload is: (a) the shared expert and its gate, (b) the hit-expert subset of the routed matmuls, if mul_mat_id were split by readiness, (c) the gate/up matmuls of the missed experts while their down tensors are still uploading (fills are queued in the order gate, up, down), and (d) state-only ops of layer il+1, which are a no-op for one sequence. At peak VRAM bandwidth that is about 50-100 us per layer, against about 1.13 ms per layer at the 2048 MiB / 22.1 tok/s point. That caps the gain from overlap at roughly 5-10%. The rest of the upload sits on the critical path router(il) -> readback/plan -> upload(il) -> routed matmul -> residual -> attn(il+1) -> router(il+1), and can only be hidden if the expert ids are known before router(il) finishes, i.e. by prediction or prefetch.

Layers with a different expert layout (blk.1, 34, 38, 39) fail llama_moe_cache_same_layout (llama-moe-cache.cpp:263) and so sit in separate cache groups with their own slot pools. Per-layer miss bytes and hit rates are not uniform, so a single 5.69 MiB per layer average hides variation.

tooling.profile_command:
PowerShell. The docs say to run the nsys CLI as administrator on Windows. Create C:\nsys first. Run the same llama args once without nsys to get a baseline tok/s.

$env:PATH = "C:\Users\steve\cuda126\bin;" + $env:PATH
$nsys = "C:\Program Files\NVIDIA Corporation\Nsight Systems 2025.6.3\target-windows-x64\nsys.exe"
& $nsys profile --trace=cuda-sw,nvtx --sample=none --cpuctxsw=none --cuda-memory-usage=false --cuda-event-trace=false --cuda-graph-trace=graph:host-only --gpu-metrics-devices=none --delay=25 --stop-on-exit=true --show-output=true --force-overwrite=true --output=C:\nsys\gen1 "C:\code\llama.cpp-fork\build\bin\llama-completion.exe" -m <model.gguf> -p "<short prompt>" -n 64 <other flags identical to the baseline>

Why each switch:
- cuda-sw: the RTX 4060 Ti (Ada) has no Hardware Event System, which is Blackwell and later. Plain 'cuda' would fall back to cuda-sw anyway and log a diagnostic, so naming cuda-sw makes the run deterministic.
- nvtx: free if the app emits no NVTX, and needed for the NVTX capture option below.
- osrt: NOT available on the Windows target. 'nsys profile --help' on this install lists cuda, cuda-sw, nvtx, cublas*, cusolver*, cusparse*, opengl*, nvvideo, vulkan*, dx11*, dx12*, openxr*, wddm, python-gil and none, with no osrt. The Windows OS-level equivalent is 'wddm' (ETW). It is system-wide, needs admin and adds overhead, so use it only in a separate diagnostic run: --trace=cuda-sw,nvtx,wddm.
- --sample=none --cpuctxsw=none: no CPU IP sampling or context-switch trace. Both add overhead and need admin on Windows. The default trace set (cuda,nvtx,opengl) is overridden, so opengl is dropped.
- --cuda-memory-usage=false and --cuda-event-trace=false: these are the defaults, written out so they stay off.
- --cuda-graph-trace=graph:host-only: the lowest-overhead graph trace. With driver 12.3 or newer the default origin is host-and-device, which the help text says may add significant overhead, and llama.cpp never launches graphs from the device.
- Default --cuda-flush-interval=0 and --cuda-trace-all-apis=false are kept.

Variant for per-kernel attribution inside llama.cpp's decode graphs (separate run, more overhead): --cuda-graph-trace=node. Alternatively keep graph-level trace and pass --env-var=GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS=1. That changes the workload (one launch per kernel, so more WDDM submissions), so treat it as a different experiment.
tooling.capture_range:
Choose one of four ways to skip the roughly 20 s model load:

1) Simplest, no code change: --delay=N. N is whole seconds of wall-clock time from launch, and collection then runs until the app exits (--stop-on-exit=true, no --duration). Do a warm-up run first so the model file is in the OS cache and load time stays steady. Set N to the observed load time plus 2-5 s. Throw away the first and last token in the window, which may be partial. CUDA injection and CUPTI start at launch even with a delay, so the load phase is not fully free of the profiler. Prompt processing may land inside the window; a short prompt and the token delimiters in (4) separate it.

2) Interactive CLI, no code change, start chosen by hand (syntax from the UserGuide examples, not checked against 'nsys launch --help'):
& $nsys launch --session-new=gen --trace=cuda-sw,nvtx --sample=none --cpuctxsw=none --cuda-graph-trace=graph:host-only "...\llama-completion.exe" <args>
In a second elevated shell, once the log shows generation has started:
& $nsys start --session=gen --output=C:\nsys\gen1 --force-overwrite=true
Then either '& $nsys stop --session=gen' or let the app exit.

3) Exact window, best option, small patch. NVTX3 is header-only in CUDA 12.6 (include\nvtx3\nvToolsExt.h) and needs no import library on Windows, because nsys sets the injection path itself. In tools\completion, put nvtxRangePushA("gen") before the first generated-token llama_decode and nvtxRangePop() after the last. Optionally wrap each llama_decode in nvtxRangePushA("tok") / nvtxRangePop() to get exact per-token buckets in NVTX_EVENTS. Profile with:
--capture-range=nvtx --nvtx-capture=gen --capture-range-end=stop-shutdown --env-var=NSYS_NVTX_PROFILER_REGISTER_ONLY=0
The env var is needed because -p matches only registered strings unless it is set to 0. Using nvtxDomainRegisterString plus -p gen@<domain> avoids it. Drop --delay when using a capture range. Equivalent alternative: cudaProfilerStart()/cudaProfilerStop() around generation with --capture-range=cudaProfilerApi --capture-range-end=stop-shutdown. That needs cudart linked into the tool or a hook exported from ggml-cuda.dll, and the docs advise a device sync before stop so buffers flush. With stop-shutdown and the default --kill=true, the app is killed when the range ends, which is fine for one run.

4) Per-token bucketing without NVTX: each decode step ends with a DtoH memcpy of the logits (copyKind=2, bytes = n_vocab*4), followed by cudaStreamSynchronize on the main thread. Use those rows as token delimiters. With GGML_CUDA_GRAPHS=ON there is also roughly one CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_GRAPH_TRACE row per GPU split per token.

tooling.sqlite_tables:
All times are int64 ns on the session clock. GPU timestamps are converted onto it.

KERNELS: CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_KERNEL
- Columns: start, end, deviceId, contextId, greenContextId, streamId, correlationId, globalPid, gridX/Y/Z, blockX/Y/Z, launchType, graphNodeId.
- correlationId links to CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_RUNTIME.correlationId.
- demangledName, shortName and mangledName are StringIds ids.
- graphNodeId is filled only with --cuda-graph-trace=node.
- With graph-level trace, kernels inside CUDA graphs are NOT in this table.

GRAPH LAUNCHES: CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_GRAPH_TRACE
- Columns: start, end, deviceId, contextId, streamId, correlationId, globalPid, graphId, graphExecId.
- One row per graph execution in graph mode. Absent in node mode, so taking the union with KERNEL never double counts.

MEMCPY: CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_MEMCPY
- Columns: start, end, deviceId, contextId, greenContextId, streamId, correlationId, globalPid, bytes, copyKind, srcKind, dstKind, srcDeviceId, srcContextId, dstDeviceId, dstContextId, migrationCause, graphNodeId, virtualAddress, copyCount.
- copyKind refers to ENUM_CUDA_MEMCPY_OPER.id; srcKind and dstKind refer to ENUM_CUDA_MEM_KIND.id.
- Memsets are in CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_MEMSET (start, end, streamId, correlationId, bytes, value, memKind refers to ENUM_CUDA_MEM_KIND).

API CALLS: CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_RUNTIME
- Columns: start, end (CPU), eventClass (0 = runtime, 1 = driver), globalTid, correlationId, nameId (refers to StringIds.id), returnValue, callchainId.
- Runtime (cuda*) and driver (cu*) calls share this table.
- StringIds names carry a version suffix (for example cudaLaunchKernel_v7000), so match with LIKE: 'cudaMemcpyAsync%', 'cudaMemcpy2DAsync%', 'cudaStreamSynchronize%', 'cudaGraphLaunch%', 'cudaLaunchKernel%', 'cudaEventRecord%', 'cudaStreamWaitEvent%'.
- Decode globalTid as PID = globalTid / 0x1000000 % 0x1000000 and TID = globalTid % 0x1000000.

SYNCHRONIZATION: CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_SYNCHRONIZATION
- Columns: start, end, streamId, correlationId, syncType (refers to ENUM_CUPTI_SYNC_TYPE), eventId, eventSyncId.

STRINGS AND ENUMS
- StringIds(id, value).
- ENUM_CUDA_MEMCPY_OPER(id, name, label).
- ENUM_CUDA_MEM_KIND(id, name, label).
- ENUM_CUPTI_SYNC_TYPE and ENUM_CUPTI_STREAM_TYPE (id, name, label).
- ENUM_NSYS_EVENT_CLASS.

STREAM, CONTEXT AND DEVICE INFO
- TARGET_INFO_CUDA_STREAM(streamId, hwId, vmId, processId, contextId, priority, flag refers to ENUM_CUPTI_STREAM_TYPE).
- TARGET_INFO_CUDA_CONTEXT_INFO(contextId, deviceId, nullStreamId).
- TARGET_INFO_GPU(id, name, busLocation, totalMemory, ...).
- TARGET_INFO_CUDA_DEVICE(gpuId, cudaId, pid).
- ggml's buffer set_tensor uses cudaStreamPerThread, and compute runs on the backend stream, so expect at least 2 streamIds.

OTHER TABLES
- NVTX: NVTX_EVENTS(start, end, eventType (59 = push/pop, 60 = start/end, 34 = mark), text, textId refers to StringIds, globalTid, domainId). The display name is COALESCE(text, StringIds.value).
- Profiler overhead: PROFILER_OVERHEAD(start, end, globalTid, nameId). Discard tokens that overlap these rows.
- ThreadNames(nameId, globalTid).

QUERY: memcpys with labels and issuing API
SELECT m.start, m.end, m.end-m.start AS dur_ns, m.bytes, ck.label AS copy, sk.label AS src, dk.label AS dst, m.streamId, s.value AS api, r.globalTid % 16777216 AS tid
FROM CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_MEMCPY m
JOIN ENUM_CUDA_MEMCPY_OPER ck ON ck.id=m.copyKind
LEFT JOIN ENUM_CUDA_MEM_KIND sk ON sk.id=m.srcKind
LEFT JOIN ENUM_CUDA_MEM_KIND dk ON dk.id=m.dstKind
LEFT JOIN CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_RUNTIME r ON r.correlationId=m.correlationId
LEFT JOIN StringIds s ON s.id=r.nameId
ORDER BY m.start;

QUERY: H2D overlap with compute on other streams
WITH h AS (SELECT rowid AS id, start, end, bytes, srcKind, streamId FROM CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_MEMCPY WHERE copyKind=1),
busy AS (SELECT start, end, streamId FROM CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_KERNEL UNION ALL SELECT start, end, streamId FROM CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_GRAPH_TRACE)
SELECT h.id, h.start, h.end-h.start AS dur_ns, h.bytes, h.srcKind, h.streamId,
 COALESCE(SUM(MAX(0, MIN(h.end,b.end)-MAX(h.start,b.start))),0) AS overlap_ns
FROM h LEFT JOIN busy b ON b.start < h.end AND b.end > h.start AND b.streamId <> h.streamId
GROUP BY h.id ORDER BY h.start;
The sum double counts only if compute intervals overlap each other. With one compute stream they do not; otherwise merge the intervals first.

QUERY: kernels with names
SELECT k.start, k.end, k.streamId, k.deviceId, s.value AS name FROM CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_KERNEL k JOIN StringIds s ON s.id=k.shortName ORDER BY k.start;

QUERY: which APIs were traced
SELECT s.value, COUNT(*), SUM(r.end-r.start) FROM CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_RUNTIME r JOIN StringIds s ON s.id=r.nameId GROUP BY s.value ORDER BY 3 DESC;

QUERY: token buckets (if NVTX added)
SELECT start, end, COALESCE(text,(SELECT value FROM StringIds WHERE id=textId)) AS name FROM NVTX_EVENTS WHERE eventType=59 ORDER BY start;
tooling.pageable_vs_pinned:
In the SQLite export, ENUM_CUDA_MEM_KIND (used by MEMCPY.srcKind/dstKind and MEMSET.memKind) is:
0 = CUDA_MEMOPR_MEMORY_KIND_PAGEABLE
1 = PINNED
2 = DEVICE
3 = ARRAY
4 = MANAGED
5 = DEVICE_STATIC
6 = MANAGED_STATIC
7 = UNKNOWN
Source: AnalysisGuide, "SQLite Schema Event Values". It is confirmed by the shipped rule target-windows-x64\rules\cuda_memcpy_async.py, which flags pageable copies with 'srcKind == 0 OR dstKind == 0'.

So:
- H2D from pageable memory: copyKind=1 AND srcKind=0 (dstKind=2 device).
- H2D from pinned memory: copyKind=1 AND srcKind=1.

Do NOT use the raw CUPTI enum CUpti_ActivityMemoryKind (UNKNOWN=0, PAGEABLE=1, PINNED=2, DEVICE=3, ...). The UserGuide quotes that enum in its memory-usage section, and it is off by one from the export.

copyKind (ENUM_CUDA_MEMCPY_OPER):
0 = unknown
1 = HtoD
2 = DtoH
3 = HtoA
4 = AtoH
5 = AtoA
6 = AtoD
7 = DtoA
8 = DtoD
9 = HtoH
10 = PtoP
11 = UVM HtoD
12 = UVM DtoH
13 = UVM DtoD

Safest practice: join the enum tables and test name/label (SELECT * FROM ENUM_CUDA_MEM_KIND; SELECT * FROM ENUM_CUDA_MEMCPY_OPER) instead of hard-coding the numbers.

How ggml host memory shows up:
- Buffers from cudaMallocHost (ggml host buffer, unless GGML_CUDA_NO_PINNED=1) report as PINNED.
- Ranges registered with cudaHostRegister (the ggml mmap path with GGML_CUDA_REGISTER_HOST=1) report as PINNED.
- Plain mmap/malloc memory reports as PAGEABLE.

Ready-made views: 'nsys stats -r cuda_gpu_trace' prints SrcMemKd/DstMemKd labels per copy, and the cuda_memcpy_async rule lists async memcpys that use pageable memory.

tooling.overhead_and_caveats:
1) WDDM batching (GeForce cannot use TCC).
- The CUDA driver on WDDM batches launches and copies into WDDM command buffers and submits them when it chooses. Work from two streams only overlaps if both reach the GPU in time.
- The GPU-side start/end values in KERNEL, MEMCPY and GRAPH_TRACE are real execution times, so overlap measured between GPU intervals is genuine.
- API-to-GPU latency (RUNTIME.end compared with kernel/memcpy start, or cuda_kern_exec_trace) is inflated and jittery. Do not judge "was the copy issued early enough" from API timestamps.
- Tracing makes every API call slower, which can move the driver's flush points.
- cudaStreamQuery/cudaEventQuery are known to force a flush on WDDM, so adding them changes behavior.
- Record the Windows Hardware-accelerated GPU scheduling (HAGS) setting with every run and never compare runs made with different settings.
- A separate --trace=wddm run (admin, system-wide ETW) shows WDDM queue packets per engine (compute versus copy) and so shows the batching directly, but it adds overhead. Do not use it for the measurement run.

2) CUPTI overhead.
- Ada has no hardware trace, so every kernel, memcpy and traced API call is instrumented in software.
- With thousands of kernels per token, tok/s will drop and gaps between kernels can widen. That can make H2D copies look more hidden (or less hidden) than they are untraced.
- Always run an untraced baseline with identical args and report the traced/untraced tok/s ratio.
- Keep the lowest-overhead settings: graph:host-only graph trace, no sampling or ctxsw, no cuda-memory-usage, no cuda-event-trace, no GPU metrics, default flush interval, default API set.
- Check PROFILER_OVERHEAD rows and the report's Diagnostics page.

3) Serialization.
- Nsight Systems records kernels in CUPTI concurrent-kernel mode. CUPTI documents CONCURRENT_KERNEL as one that "doesn't break kernel concurrency", whereas plain KERNEL mode serializes. The export table is still named CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_KERNEL.
- Memcpy tracing does not force copies to serialize with kernels.
- Things that can bias overlap downward:
  - --cuda-graph-trace=node: per-node overhead, and the 2025.6 release notes say cross-stream parallelism may be reduced.
  - --cuda-event-trace=true: uses timing events, which can create false cross-stream dependencies. Keep it false; it also requires CUDA UMD 12.8 or newer.
  - GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS=1: a different workload with many more WDDM submissions.

4) llama.cpp CUDA graphs (GGML_CUDA_GRAPHS=ON in this build).
- In graph mode, decode kernels and any memcpy nodes captured inside a graph are invisible individually. Only GRAPH_TRACE spans exist.
- Treat GRAPH_TRACE spans as busy-compute time. This is conservative, because the spans include idle gaps inside the graph.
- Use a node-mode run only for per-kernel attribution.

5) Pageable sources.
- cudaMemcpyAsync from pageable memory is staged by the driver through pinned bounce buffers and is effectively synchronous to the calling host thread.
- The GPU-side MEMCPY interval covers all staged chunks, so its apparent GB/s is low and its interval overstates DMA busy time. Overlap figures for pageable copies therefore overstate real transfer overlap.
- The host thread is blocked during the copy (a long cudaMemcpyAsync row in RUNTIME), so any overlap comes from work already queued or from another thread.
- ggml's buffer set_tensor does cudaMemcpyAsync on cudaStreamPerThread followed by cudaStreamSynchronize, so it blocks the host even with pinned memory.

6) Clocks. Compare GPU intervals with GPU intervals (memcpy against kernel or graph); both come from the same GPU clock. Avoid fine conclusions from CPU-API-against-GPU timestamps.

7) VRAM. The release notes say CUDA trace needs some GPU memory and can fail or break an app that uses all of it. On the 8 GB RTX 4060 Ti with an expert cache sized to fill VRAM, leave a few hundred MB of headroom, and use the same cache size for the baseline.

8) Capture window.
- --delay counts wall-clock time from launch, while injection and CUPTI init still happen at launch.
- Model load time varies with the OS file cache, so warm it up first.
- Discard the first and last token in the window and separate prompt processing (batch > 1, where ggml disables graphs) from decode.
- Keep -n at 32-128 tokens. Sessions longer than about 5 minutes are not supported.

9) Export.
- Rows are not guaranteed to be in time order (2025.6 release notes), so always ORDER BY.
- Tables are lazy unless --lazy=false.
- The schema can change between versions; check META_DATA_EXPORT.

10) Privileges. The UserGuide says to run the CLI as administrator on Windows. Sampling, cpuctxsw, --isr and wddm trace need admin; -s none and --cpuctxsw=none avoid them.

11) Doc inconsistency. The local UserGuide list "CUDA Runtime API Calls Skipped by Default" (456 names) includes cudaMemcpyAsync, cudaLaunchKernel, cudaStreamSynchronize, cudaEventRecord and cudaStreamWaitEvent. That contradicts the shipped rules and doc examples, which rely on those calls being traced. Verify on the first capture with the distinct-API-name query. If a needed API is missing, use --cuda-trace-all-apis=true, which costs more overhead.

12) Release notes describe a driver bug where default hardware CUDA trace collects no events. It does not apply to Ada, which uses software trace, but it is one more reason to pin --trace=cuda-sw.

13) PATH. nsys inherits the caller's environment (-n true), so prepend C:\Users\steve\cuda126\bin in the shell. --env-var=PATH=... would replace PATH entirely.
